description:
In 2022, Shein was valued at around $100 billion and was the most downloaded shopping app in America. It sold $5 tops and $10 dresses, added thousands of new styles every day, and turned haul videos into a global phenomenon. But behind the cheap prices were years of controversies over labor conditions, copied designs, cotton sourcing, waste, and a tax loophole that let its parcels into the US duty free. In 2025 and 2026, the world finally pushed back.
 
In this video, we break down how a secretive Chinese entrepreneur turned an online wedding dress business into the biggest fast fashion company on the planet, and how Shein is now facing the consequences. We cover Chris Xu's data driven model, the de minimis loophole, the Channel 4 documentary and labor investigations, the designer lawsuits, the Xinjiang cotton questions, the Paris store scandal, the EU investigation, and Shein's long awaited Hong Kong IPO at a valuation 70% below its peak.

title: From $250 Billion To Nothing: How Nokia Lost Everything
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
In 2000, Nokia was the most valuable company in Europe, worth roughly $250 billion. It sold more phones than anyone on Earth, its ringtone was everywhere, and the Nokia 3310 became a legend for being indestructible. Just over a decade later, its phone business was collapsing, and in 2013, Nokia sold it to Microsoft for around €5.4 billion.
 
In this video, we break down how a 150 year old Finnish company that started out making paper and rubber boots became the king of mobile phones, and how it lost everything. We cover Fredrik Idestam's pulp mill, Jorma Ollila's bet on telecoms, the GSM revolution, Snake and the 3310, the arrival of the iPhone and Android, the Symbian and MeeGo struggles, Stephen Elop's burning platform memo, the Windows Phone gamble, the Microsoft sale and Nokia's surprising new life in AI networking.

title: $2.1 Billion To Forgotten: How Supreme Lost Everything

description:
In December 2020, Supreme was sold for $2.1 billion. It was the undisputed king of streetwear, the brand that turned a red box logo into a status symbol and convinced people to fight over a $30 brick. Less than four years later, it was sold again for $1.5 billion, a loss of roughly $600 million.
 
In this video, we break down how Supreme went from a tiny skate shop on Lafayette Street in New York to a billion dollar hype machine, and how that hype slowly disappeared. We cover James Jebbia's founding of the brand in 1994, the scarcity strategy behind Thursday drops and resale madness, the legendary Louis Vuitton collaboration, and the corporate deals with Carlyle, VF Corporation and EssilorLuxottica that changed everything.
 
You'll learn:
- How Supreme built the most powerful hype machine in fashion history
- Why the Carlyle and VF deals damaged Supreme's rebellious image
- How Supreme's share of the StockX resale market fell by more than half

How smartphones, DJI and Insta360 stole GoPro's customers
Why GoPro's patent battle against Insta360 mostly failed

description:
In June 2008, BlackBerry was worth $83 billion. Within a few short years, it was writing off nearly a billion dollars of unsold phones, searching for a buyer, and eventually giving up on making phones altogether.
 
In this video, we break down how BlackBerry went from a tiny Canadian engineering firm called Research In Motion to the most powerful phone brand on Earth, and how it lost everything. We cover Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie's partnership, the rise of push email and BBM, the iPhone moment that changed everything, and the string of mistakes that followed.
 
You'll learn:
How BlackBerry invented the modern smartphone experience years before the iPhone
Why BlackBerry's leaders underestimated the iPhone and Android
How the BlackBerry Storm, the PlayBook and the 2011 global outage destroyed trust
Why BlackBerry 10 arrived far too late and led to a $965 million write-down

What BlackBerry looks like today as a car software company built around QNX
 
Was BlackBerry's fall inevitable, or could it have survived the smartphone revolution? Let us know what you think in the comments.

From the 1987 buyout and the Japanese rescue to the Speedway acquisition, worker exploitation cases, the Australian wage scandal, the Couche-Tard takeover battle, the FTC penalty, 645 planned closures, and its push toward food-forward stores, this is a story about what happens when a company believes being everywhere is enough.

title: How Credit Card Companies Actually Make Money
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
You tap your card for a 5 dollar coffee. The coffee shop receives 4.88. The 12 cents that disappeared in under a second went to the bank that issued your card. That happens on every transaction. on every purchase. at every merchant. And in 2025 it added up to a record 198.25 billion dollars in card processing fees paid by US merchants alone according to the Merchant Payments Coalition citing Nilson Report data. That number has more than tripled since 2009.
 
This video follows the money through every layer of the credit card business. It starts with interchange. the 1 to 2 percent fee that flows from every merchant to your issuing bank on every transaction according to Citibank Credit Card Issuance Trust SEC filings and established network practice. and explains how the Visa and Mastercard combined average credit card interchange rate reached 2.36 percent in 2025. It covers the 174 billion dollars in credit card interest income the entire US banking industry recorded in 2024 according to Congressional Research Service data. why the five largest issuers charged APRs 8 to 10 percentage points higher than small banks and credit unions for the same accounts according to the CFPB. and why the share of cardholders making only the minimum payment is at its highest level since at least 2015 per the CFPB 2025 Credit Card Market Report. It explains why Visa generated 35.9 billion dollars in net revenues and Mastercard generated 28.2 billion dollars in fiscal 2025 without lending a single dollar or issuing a single card. why the rewards on your premium card were funded by the merchant fee paid by the store you bought your coffee from. and how a National Bureau of Economic Research analysis published in July 2026 found that interchange fees transfer approximately 30 billion dollars annually from cash users to credit card users and approximately 9.2 billion dollars annually from households earning under 150,000 dollars to those earning more.

title: How Car Dealerships Make Money
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
A car dealership doesn't make money selling cars. The average gross profit on a new domestic vehicle in 2024 was 2.247 dollars per unit according to Presidio-NCM data from nearly 3.900 US dealerships. That number disappears the moment you factor in floor plan interest. The money is somewhere else entirely — and it is in a room most people walk through without realizing what just happened.

This video follows the money through every layer of the car dealership business. It starts with why the new car on the lot generates the thinnest margin in the building. explains the floor plan loan system where every unsold vehicle costs the dealer money every single day it sits. covers the F&I office where a forty-minute conversation about warranties and loan rates generates more gross profit per vehicle than the car sale itself. reveals how dealer rate markup works on financing and why the interest rate you were offered may not be the rate the bank actually approved. and ends in the service department. where 276 million repair orders generated 164 billion dollars in service and parts revenue across America's franchised dealerships in 2025 per NADA data. at gross margins of 45 to 70 percent that the sales floor cannot match on its best day.

The car is not the product. The car is how they get you in the building.

title: The Economics Of Owning a Gym
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Most people think owning a gym is about passion for fitness and filling the floor with motivated members. The reality is far more interesting. The gym industry is built on a structural advantage unlike almost any other consumer business: 67 percent of members pay their monthly fee without visiting regularly or at all, which means the most profitable gym member is the one who signs up in January and never comes back.

This video breaks down the complete economics of owning a gym in 2026, starting with the real startup costs, which range from 50,000 dollars for a lean specialty studio to well over 500,000 dollars for a full-service health club. It covers the lease and buildout trap that quietly doubles most first-time owners' budgets, why used equipment from gym liquidations can save tens of thousands of dollars, and the shipping costs that almost nobody budgets for.

From there it explains the operating leverage of the membership model, why personal training at 40 to 60 percent gross margin is the real profit engine, and why June kills more gyms than January saves them. It covers the real failure rate, why approximately 50 percent of gyms do not survive five years almost never because of bad fitness programming but almost always because of bad financial planning, and ends with verified profit numbers for two realistic scenarios: a boutique studio and a mid-size independent gym.

This video introduces a three-part framework, timing, insight, and systems, that cuts through all of that.
